introduction-the-4kb-problem.core: Linux manages memory in 4 KB pages by default. A process using 64 GB needs about 16 million page-table entries, and the CPU's TLB (the cache of address translations) holds only a few thousand, so large-memory workloads (databases, JVMs, caches) constantly miss the TLB and walk page tables, wasting cycles. Huge pages (2 MB or 1 GB) cut the number of translations by 512× or 262,144×.

first_principles.problem: A 128 GB in-memory database spends 15% of CPU on page-table walks.
truths: Bigger pages cover more memory per entry.
derivation: Use **2 MB pages** for big heaps.
Consider **1 GB pages** for huge fixed allocations.

analogy.title: Street addresses vs postcodes
analogy.story: Looking up every house individually is slow; looking up whole postcodes needs far fewer entries in your address book.
analogy.breaks: Postcodes are fixed; huge pages must be contiguous physical memory.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Shows why huge pages slash TLB misses.

points: 4 KB too small for big heaps.

check.q: Why do huge pages improve performance for large-memory applications?
check.a: Each TLB entry covers far more memory, drastically reducing TLB misses and page-table walks.

the-tlb-why-page-size-determines-cpu-spe.core: Every virtual address must be translated to a physical one. The TLB caches recent translations; on a miss the hardware walks a 4- or 5-level page table in memory, up to 4 or 5 dependent memory reads, though some may hit cache. TLB reach (entries × page size) determines how much memory can be accessed without misses: 1,536 entries × 4 KB is 6 MB, but × 2 MB is 3 GB. Random access over large datasets suffers most.

first_principles.problem: Hash-table lookups across 50 GB are slow even though the hash function is fast.
truths: Page walks are dependent memory reads.
derivation: Use **huge pages** when working set ≫ reach.

analogy.title: A receptionist's speed-dial list
analogy.story: Numbers on speed dial connect instantly; others need looking up in a thick directory with several indexes.
analogy.breaks: Directories don't nest 5 deep; page tables do, and in VMs it doubles.

code.text:
perf stat -e dTLB-loads,dTLB-load-misses,page-faults ./hashbench
# dTLB-load-misses: 18% of loads   → TLB-bound
# after enabling 2 MB pages: 0.4%

check.a: The total memory addressable without TLB misses: number of TLB entries multiplied by the page size.

explicit-hugepages-hugetlb.core: Explicit huge pages (hugetlbfs) are reserved in advance via vm.nr_hugepages or the kernel boot line, removed from the general pool and never swapped. Applications request them with mmap(MAP_HUGETLB), shmget(SHM_HUGETLB) or files on a hugetlbfs mount. They're guaranteed and predictable, with no compaction delays, but the memory is unavailable to anything else and must be sized correctly, since allocation fails if there aren't enough.

first_principles.problem: A database needs guaranteed huge pages at startup without unpredictable latency from the kernel.

analogy.title: Reserving a private dining room
analogy.story: Booked in advance and guaranteed for your party, but nobody else can use it even when you're not there.
analogy.breaks: Rooms can be re-let at short notice; reserved pages stay reserved.

code.text:
sysctl -w vm.nr_hugepages=16384           # 16384 × 2 MB = 32 GB
echo 'vm.nr_hugepages=16384' > /etc/sysctl.d/90-hugepages.conf
grep -i huge /proc/meminfo
# HugePages_Total: 16384  HugePages_Free: 16384  Hugepagesize: 2048 kB

check.q: Why reserve explicit huge pages at boot rather than later?
check.a: Memory becomes fragmented over time, so the kernel may be unable to find enough contiguous 2 MB regions later.

transparent-hugepages-thp.core: Transparent Huge Pages let the kernel automatically back anonymous memory with 2 MB pages when aligned and available, and khugepaged collapses 4 KB pages into huge pages in the background. It needs no app changes, but compaction stalls, memory bloat (a 2 MB page for sparse use) and khugepaged CPU can cause latency spikes. Many databases (Redis, MongoDB, Oracle) recommend 'madvise' or 'never' rather than 'always'.

first_principles.problem: Redis shows periodic 100 ms latency spikes traced to THP compaction.

analogy.title: An automatic furniture upgrade service
analogy.story: It swaps your small tables for big ones when it can, but sometimes rearranges the room while you're trying to eat.
analogy.breaks: Furniture swaps are visible; THP stalls are invisible latency.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Latency spikes gone; opted-in apps still benefit.

code.text:
cat /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled     # [always] madvise never
echo madvise > /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled
echo defer+madvise > /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/defrag
grep AnonHugePages /proc/meminfo
grep thp_ /proc/vmstat | head

check.q: Why do many databases recommend disabling THP or using madvise?
check.a: THP compaction and khugepaged activity can cause unpredictable latency spikes and memory bloat.

one-gigabyte-pages-1gb-hugepages.core: 1 GB huge pages give the maximum TLB reach. A few dozen entries cover tens of gigabytes, ideal for very large, long-lived, fixed allocations: VM guest memory, DPDK packet buffers, large database buffer pools and in-memory analytics. They must be reserved at boot (default_hugepagesz=1G hugepagesz=1G hugepages=N) because finding contiguous 1 GB regions later is practically impossible. They're only for explicit hugetlbfs, never THP.

first_principles.problem: A hypervisor hosting large VMs wants to minimise nested page-walk overhead.

analogy.title: Renting whole floors instead of rooms
analogy.story: Few contracts to manage, but you need to book early and can't rent half a floor.
analogy.breaks: Floors can be sublet; 1 GB pages can't be split for other uses.

example.title: Boot config

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: 64 GB backed by just 64 TLB entries.

code.text:
grep -o pdpe1gb /proc/cpuinfo | head -1
# /etc/default/grub
# GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX="default_hugepagesz=1G hugepagesz=1G hugepages=64"
update-grub && reboot
mount -t hugetlbfs -o pagesize=1G none /dev/hugepages1G

example.outcome: maximum TLB reach for big allocations.

check.q: Why must 1 GB huge pages usually be reserved on the kernel command line?
check.a: After boot, memory fragments and the kernel can rarely find contiguous, aligned 1 GB physical regions.

calculating-the-right-vmnr_hugepages-val.core: Size the explicit huge-page pool to what applications will actually map: the database's shared buffers, JVM heap, or DPDK pools, plus a small overhead margin, divided by the page size. Too few and the app fails to start or silently falls back to 4 KB pages; too many and the reserved memory is wasted and can starve the OS. On NUMA systems, reserve per node. Verify after startup that HugePages_Free is near zero and HugePages_Rsvd is accounted for.

first_principles.problem: PostgreSQL starts without huge pages because nr_hugepages was 10% too small, and nobody notices.

analogy.title: Booking hotel rooms for a conference
analogy.story: Count attendees plus a couple of spares; too few and people are turned away, too many and you pay for empty rooms.
analogy.breaks: Hotels refund sometimes; reserved RAM is just unavailable.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Exact pool; startup fails loudly if wrong.

code.text:
postgres -D $PGDATA -C shared_memory_size_in_huge_pages   # e.g. 16450
sysctl -w vm.nr_hugepages=16500
# postgresql.conf: huge_pages = on   (fail rather than silently fall back)
grep -E 'HugePages_(Total|Free|Rsvd)' /proc/meminfo

check.q: Why set PostgreSQL's huge_pages to 'on' instead of 'try'?
check.a: So startup fails loudly if huge pages aren't available, rather than silently falling back to 4 KB pages.

configuring-postgres-for-hugepages.core: PostgreSQL's shared_buffers and other shared memory live in one large segment, a prime candidate for huge pages. Set huge_pages = on (or try), size vm.nr_hugepages from shared_memory_size_in_huge_pages, optionally set huge_page_size, ensure the postgres user's memlock limits allow it under systemd, and set THP to madvise or never. Benefits are fewer TLB misses and smaller page tables per backend process, important with many connections.

first_principles.problem: A Postgres server with 500 connections uses 20 GB just for page tables because each backend maps shared_buffers with 4 KB pages.

analogy.title: Every employee carrying a map of the shared warehouse
analogy.story: With street-level detail each map is huge; with a district-level map it's tiny.
analogy.breaks: Paper maps are copied; page tables are rebuilt per process.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: ~19 GB of RAM reclaimed from page tables.

code.text:
# before: shared_buffers=32GB, 500 backends
grep PageTables /proc/meminfo     # PageTables: 19876543 kB
# after huge_pages=on
grep PageTables /proc/meminfo     # PageTables: 412345 kB
grep -E 'HugePages_(Free|Rsvd)' /proc/meminfo

check.q: Why do huge pages especially help PostgreSQL with many connections?
check.a: Each backend process maps shared_buffers; with 4 KB pages each needs huge page tables, which huge pages shrink dramatically.

configuring-java-jvm-for-hugepages.core: Large JVM heaps benefit from huge pages too. -XX:+UseLargePages uses explicit hugetlbfs pages (sized via nr_hugepages to cover -Xmx plus metaspace and code cache margin); -XX:+UseTransparentHugePages asks for THP via madvise (with THP enabled=madvise); -XX:LargePageSizeInBytes=1g selects 1 GB pages. Pair with -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch to fault the heap in at startup, avoiding page faults and latency later.

first_principles.problem: A 64 GB-heap trading JVM shows GC pause variance linked to TLB misses and page faults.
truths: JVM heaps are large, contiguous regions.
THP via madvise is safer than always.

analogy.title: Laying out a large exhibition hall in advance
analogy.story: Set up all the stands before doors open, using big floor sections, so nothing has to be rearranged during the show.
analogy.breaks: Halls can be expanded; fixed heaps can't grow beyond -Xmx.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Stable latency; heap backed by 2 MB pages.

check.a: Touches every heap page at JVM startup so memory is faulted in (and huge pages allocated) before the application runs, avoiding later page-fault latency.
